newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan investors seen sidelined at US note auction.
newsitem.headline: Japan investors seen sidelined at US note auction.

text.p: Japanese investors are expected to be sidelined at the 10-year U.S. Treasury note auction scheduled for Tuesday, market sources said on Monday.

Japanese operators are expected to hold back from active purchasing at the 10-year auction as U.S. Treasury prices in general have climbed rapidly after last Friday's payroll data and because of the dollar's continued strength, they said.

"There are no definite reasons to buy at the upcoming 10-year note auction," said a senior official at a major life insurance firm. "We don't need to stand out at the auction. We are always ready to buy regularly, but we can wait a little."

The official added his company might have to raise the volume of its investment in Treasuries, taking into consideration the low domestic market interest rates, although the dollar/yen rate and current bond price levels make it difficult to actively invest its funds at the note auction.
Up until the early 1990s, Japanese life insurance firms were big investors in the U.S. Treasury market. They would often purchase 20 to 30 percent of the total offering at an auction.
But the buying boom came to a halt as they cut back on foreign bond investments after profits were battered, mainly because of the yen's sharp appreciation.
Another official with a Japanese institutional investor said: "Underlying fundamentals look strong, but we are not thinking about bidding actively at the auction."
"We feel that prices are still in the higher end of a boxed range. We can wait a bit before a series of key economic indicators later this week and next week to determine the trends," he said.
Japanese operators' investment in U.S. Treasuries has stood out in recent weeks as they were seen shifting more funds into the U.S. market, helped in part by the dollar's recent surge to 112 yen.

"Except for the quarterly refunding, Japanese investors have not been very active about participating in auctions...particularly for ones with longer durations," a senior trader at a major brokerage house said. "But an attitude of buying on dips is expected to remain strong."
